prompt:
Here's a post-incident writeup I drafted with Claude's help. It uses a lot of "may," "could," and "we don't know yet" because we genuinely don't have root cause nailed down. But I want to make sure the uncertainty is doing real work in the writing and not just serving as cover. Where should I commit harder, and where is the uncertainty actually earned?

Input files: incident_writeup.md
assertions: The audit flags the sentence in §Mitigation efficacy — "Something that may be oversimplifying but worth noting: the fact that failover resolved the symptom does not mean the cause is region-specific" — as an evasive pre-apology (pattern #7). The claim that follows is substantive and correct; the "may be oversimplifying but worth noting" prefix adds generic deniability without naming a specific limit on the reasoning.

The audit flags question 4 in §Open questions — "The fact of the matter is this is complicated and touches on deeper questions about how we want to handle load-shedding... Some would argue for it, others would argue against" — as a meta-descent (pattern #3). The on-call does have a position they could state, or at least a concrete tradeoff to name; "this is complicated" is covering for not stating it.

The audit does NOT flag the §What we do not know yet section's hedges as evasive. Phrases like "whether the p99 increase is the cause or symptom," "the logs do not disambiguate these two possibilities," "too small to be causal," and "a git-blame review of the touched files is pending" are earned — each hedge names a specific uncertainty the author is tracking rather than hiding behind.

The audit does NOT flag the §What we know bullet about the 2026-11-03 logging refactor — "a delayed effect from that change can't be ruled out but has no supporting evidence yet" — as evasive. This is an earned hedge: it names what the author considered, what they found, and why the question is still open.

The audit, in aggregate, correctly discriminates earned from evasive hedges. A failing audit would either flag most or all hedges as evasive (which would misread the document — most of the hedges here are tracking real unresolved questions) or flag none (which would miss the two genuine evasions in §Mitigation efficacy and §Open questions #4). The audit should produce an "Earned hedges" section listing several earned uncertainties, alongside the 1-2 evasive flags.
